1:
Three pounce on the word fellow-elder, and a fourth refuses to let them. Henry notes how different the spirit of Peter was from that of his pretended successors: he does not command and domineer but exhort, nor style himself prince of the apostles or head of the church, but values himself upon being an elder — all the apostles were elders, though every elder was not an apostle. Clarke asks it directly: had he been what the popes of Rome say he was, could he have spoken of himself as he does here? The popes and the Scriptures, he adds, never agree. Barnes makes the same point more quietly: Peter does not put his exhortation on the ground of apostolical authority, or because he was head of the church — would he have used this language if he had been?

Ellicott dissents. Peter is giving no irresponsible advice: he is the head Christian of the world, writing from the thick of the persecution begun in Rome, so the Asiatic elders cannot set his advice down as that of some easy layman. It can hardly be said, therefore, that this is an example of humility; the effect is rather to make the recipients feel that he is using a strong argument from the greater to the less.

On the office they agree, against the same target. Barnes observes that only one class of ministers is addressed, with no mention of three orders of bishops, priests and deacons, and that the words episcopate, episcopal and episcopacy are merely the Greek word of this verse transferred into our language, so that the duties of the episcopate pertained to those called elders. Clarke calls it another proof that bishop and presbyter were the same order in apostolic times, though afterwards made distinct. Calvin says the two names are synonymous, and that they were called elders for honour’s sake, not because all were old, but because they were principally chosen from the aged, who have more prudence and experience. Gill adds that the title is not always literal, since young men such as Timothy were chosen into the office, the same with that of pastors, bishops or overseers.

Feed is the word that carries the memory. Ellicott says there is hardly any doubt Peter was thinking of the scene by the sea, since the Lord had committed into his hands all his sheep and lambs without restriction of age or country; and now, the time approaching when he must put off this tabernacle, he takes order that the charge be fulfilled after his death — he still shepherds the flock by proxy. Robertson confirms it from the vocabulary: Jesus used this very word to Peter in the interview by the Sea of Galilee. Clarke says it in a phrase: do not fleece the flock.

Calvin finds three vices in the way and sets a virtue against each: against sloth, alacrity; against desire of gain, liberality; against lust for power, moderation. He is sharpest on the third: what stands opposed to it is tyrannical pride, when the pastor exempts himself from all subjection and tyrannizes over the Church, and this cannot be corrected except their authority be restrained. On filthy lucre the three answer differently. Robertson draws a flat inference: clearly the elders received stipends, else there could be no such temptation. Clarke doubts it, asking whether the office of a bishop in those days of persecution could be lucrative at all, and whether the Spirit does not lead the apostle to speak rather for posterity than for that time. Wesley applies it to his own country and loses his temper: consider this, ye that leave one flock and go to another merely because there is more gain, a larger salary — is it not astonishing that men see no harm in this, that it is not only practised but avowed all over the nation?
3:
The prohibited verb divides them. Barnes takes it strictly: the word refers to the jurisdiction civil rulers exercise, authority as distinguished from the influence of reason and example, so that the command prohibits all assumption of temporal power by ministers of religion — a command, he adds, very little regarded in the church. Ellicott will not have it so strictly: the English is too strong for the Greek, since there is a sense in which the heads of the Church are and ought to be lords over the rest, and that is very different from lording it, acting tyrannically.

On the noun rendered heritage several converge, and the word turns out to be a small history. Ellicott traces it: first the actual scrap of paper or wood tossed; then, as with the word lot in auctions, the property that falls by lot; then, all notion of chance gone, the portion assigned to anyone. So the lots here are the congregations and parishes allotted to the elders — and our version misleads, he says, in substituting a singular for the plural and inserting the word God’s. Wesley reaches the same: the word is literally the portions; there is one flock under one chief Shepherd, but many portions of it under many pastors. Robertson supplies its English descent, that from the adjective come our cleric, clerical and clerk, and that Wycliffe rendered the clause, neither as having lordship in the clergie.

Which raises the question the word always carries. Barnes reports that some took it of the clergy, priests and deacons under a bishop, and remarks drily that such an interpretation would hardly be adopted now. Calvin is less patient: some very ignorantly think that those called clergy are meant here; it was an ancient way of speaking to call the whole order of ministers clergy, but I wish it had never occurred to the Fathers to speak thus, for what Scripture ascribes to the whole Church it was by no means right to confine to a few men. Gill says it plainly: the word clergy is common to all the saints, not to be appropriated to a particular order of men.

Clarke turns the ensamples into a shape: they are types, moulds of a heavenly form, into which the spirits and lives of the flock may be cast, that they come out after a perfect pattern; and asks whether the churches which profess to be reformed keep the advice any better than the church that arrogates the title Catholic: are they lords over the heritage, disputing with their flocks about penny-farthing tithes rather than contending for the faith once delivered to the saints? Ellicott offers colder comfort: it is some consolation, when we groan under the lives of some church officers now, that even in the apostles’ days cowardice, greed and self-assertion were not unknown — and quotes the poet’s parson, who taught Christ’s lore and his apostles twelve, but first practised it himself.

The title chief Shepherd seems the apostle’s own coinage. Ellicott thinks he invented it, and asks how an office could be more honoured than by speaking of Christ as the chief bearer of it. On the crown he and Robertson both go to the flower. It is an amaranth, Ellicott says, a flower which like our immortelles does not lose colour or form — though he cautions us not to think too literally of the wreath. Robertson adds why the plant earned the name: it never withers, and revives if moistened with water, and so was a symbol of immortality. Calvin ends on why the promise is needed: pastors have often to do with ungrateful men from whom they receive an unworthy reward, long labours are often in vain, and Satan sometimes prevails — so for the servant of Christ there is one and only one remedy, to turn his eyes to the coming of Christ.
5:
Who are the younger? Most take it of standing rather than years. Gill says all the members of churches in common are meant, as distinct from their officers; Henry notes the term was used by our Saviour to signify an inferior; Clarke glosses it as those not in sacred offices. Ellicott presses it furthest: the lay people are styled juniors beside the presbyters although in natural age they might be older, just as our Lord addressed his disciples as children though several were older than himself — though he allows that it may mean those in inferior offices, deacons, catechists and readers. Robertson dissents flatly: the antithesis between younger and elder shows the word here refers to age, not office as in the first verse.

The verb for being clothed is rare, and four work on it. Barnes derives it from a strip or loop for fastening a garment, and notes that the related noun means a long white apron worn by slaves. Clarke knows the ornamental sense — an outer garment tied with bows of coloured ribands — but inclines to the servile one, since the apostle wants them to put on humility as the servant’s dress, and the next clause proves he cannot mean an ornament. Ellicott renders it, tie yourselves up in humility: it is gathered tight round about us like a cloak and tied so the wind may not blow it back. Robertson supplies what the others miss: it is quite probable Peter is thinking of what Jesus did when he girded himself with a towel and taught the disciples, Peter in particular, the lesson of humility. Peter, he adds, had at last learned it.

Ellicott adds that the true text strikes out the words be subject and, so the clause runs, all of you be clothed with humility one to another — not only between rulers and ruled, but clergy to clergy and laity to laity. Henry states why the duty matters: humility is the great preserver of peace and order in all Christian churches, and consequently pride is the great disturber.

Then the mighty hand, where two read opposite things into it. Barnes takes it of chastisement, referring to the calamities God had brought upon them: when that hand was upon them they were not to be lifted up with pride, and there is no situation in which one is more likely to feel humility than in scenes of affliction. Ellicott denies it: the mighty hand is not that which chastises them, but the protecting shelter they are humbly to seek. Wesley says only that the hand of God is in all troubles. On the promised exaltation Barnes allows both a present and a future fulfilment, Ellicott expects the day of judgment which seemed so instant, and Calvin declines to be hurried: we must learn humility now, but the Lord well knows when it is expedient for us to be elevated.

Calvin raises the objection nobody else does. Whence come the proverbs that we shall have to howl among wolves, and that they are foolish who are like sheep exposing themselves to wolves, except that we think our humility sets loose the reins to the audacity of the ungodly? But this fear, he answers, arises from our ignorance of divine providence; as soon as we are convinced God cares for us, our minds are easily led to patience and humility. Clarke reads the closing clause the same way: God meddles or concerns himself with the things that interest us, so he who knows God cares for him need have no anxious cares about himself. Ellicott locates the fault: anxiety implies not only some distrust of God’s providence but also some belief that we could manage better for ourselves. He adds a caution: the play on the word care in the English represents nothing in the original, where the two words are quite different.
8:
Clarke finds an apposition in the verse that he thinks nobody has noticed. Be sober is built from a word meaning not to swallow down, and the verb at the far end of the verse means to gulp down. So the warning turns on itself: it is not every one the enemy can swallow, for the sober are proof against him, while those drunken with the cares of this world he may swallow down. He glosses the pair plainly: avoid drunkenness of your senses and of your souls; awake and keep awake, for your enemies are alert and never off their guard. Gill notes that both were urged before and are repeated here, the one not well being without the other. Wesley draws the connexion the other way, to the verse before: there is a close connexion between watching and the duly casting of our care upon him — and how deeply, he adds, had Peter himself suffered for want of watching.

Ellicott hears the tone of the two words. They are single words in the Greek, in the tense that bespeaks immediate attention — the sudden cries of a shepherd who spies the lion prowling round the flock in the darkness while the guardians lie drowsy; and the apostle is not observing that Satan always prowls, but warning the sleeping shepherds that he is especially doing so now, this season of persecution being his time for picking off one and another. Barnes makes the point from the animal: this is not the crouching lion creeping towards his foe, but the raging monarch of the woods, whose terrible roar would intimidate all so that they might become an easy prey.

Henry takes the title apart: the word rendered devil derives from one signifying to strike through, or to stab, and he would strike malignity into our natures and poison into our souls. Clarke sorts the enemy’s methods into three: the subtle serpent, to beguile our senses; the angel of light, to deceive us with false views of spiritual things; and the roaring lion, to bear us down by violent opposition, persecution and death, which is how he was then acting towards the sufferers in Pontus.

Cyril of Jerusalem works that middle form at length. Vice mimics virtue, and the tares strive to be thought wheat, growing like wheat in appearance but detected by good judges from the taste. The devil transfigures himself into an angel of light — not that he may reascend to where he was, for having made his heart hard as an anvil he has a will that cannot repent, but that he may envelope those living an angelic life in a mist of blindness. Many wolves go about in sheep’s clothing, their clothing being that of sheep but not so their claws and teeth. We have need therefore of a sober mind and eyes that see, lest taking the wolf for a sheep we become his prey.

On resisting, Ellicott reads a formation as well as a posture: stand and face him, rather than running from posts of duty or lying still and letting things take their course; and the words for stedfast in the faith seem to mean not only that each is to stand firm but that all together are to present a solid front to the lion. Calvin supplies the ground of the confidence: there is sufficient strength in faith, since faith alone is our victory over the world. Robertson puts it in eight words — cowardice never wins against the devil, but only courage — and finds in the next clause an unusual construction, as though the sufferings were a tax being paid. Ellicott quotes an archbishop: some Christians are ready to think there was never any beloved of God in such a condition as theirs — whereas the whole brotherhood go in this way, and our eldest Brother went first.
10:
Gill unpacks the title: God has treasured up a fulness of grace in his Son and is the author of electing, adopting and regenerating grace; he is so described here to encourage souls to come to the throne of grace and expect a sufficiency in every time of need. Barnes adds that such a prayer from an apostle would itself be a pledge that the grace would be granted. Clarke supplies the strangest parallel in the chapter — Mohammed conveys this same description in the words opening all but two chapters of his Koran, whose best translation is the apostle’s own: the God of all grace, most merciful and most compassionate. Calvin turns the verse on the ministry: doctrine is in vain poured forth into the air unless God works by his Spirit, and ministers ought to pray that he give success to their labours, for otherwise they effect nothing by planting or watering.

Four verbs follow, and Clarke takes every one as a building term. Make perfect is to put you in complete joint, as the timbers of a building; stablish, to adapt you strongly to each other so that you may be mutual supports; strengthen, to cramp and bind every part against warping or splitting; settle, to cause all to rest so evenly on the surest foundation that you may grow together to a holy temple. All these phrases are architectural, he says, the apostle having again in view the living stones of his second chapter. Barnes gets the same picture from the last verb: it means literally to found you, on ground no wind or flood will move. Wesley glosses the last, settle you as an house upon a rock; Robertson notes that the third is a word found nowhere else.

Whether the sentence prays or promises turns on the text. Calvin reports that some copies have the future, as though a promise were made, but that the other reading is more commonly received, and keeps it prayer. Clarke takes the futures — all these words are so read by the best manuscripts and versions: he will make you perfect — and Ellicott agrees, adding that the true reading is who called you, not us.

On the little while, Barnes allows it of time or of degree, both being true: afflictions are short compared with eternity and light compared with the weight of glory. Ellicott presses the Greek — it looks as if Peter meant not only after you have suffered but by the fact of your having suffered — and draws an inference nobody else draws: he seems to contemplate the persecution passing off before the end of the world, for these verbs could hardly be used of our education in the world to come. Henry keeps to what is asked: the apostle prays not that they be excused from sufferings but that these be moderate and short, and that God would settle them so firmly upon Christ that their union might be indissoluble; perseverance is so difficult a work that only the God of all grace can accomplish it. Wesley divides the labour bluntly: ye have only to watch and resist the devil, the rest God will perform; and he hears the apostle, being converted, strengthening his brethren.

The doxology is brief. Gill notes that the Syriac begins it in the previous verse, and takes the Amen as signifying that so the apostle prayed it might be and believed it would. Robertson observes that it is briefer than the one closing the fourth chapter, addressed to Christ. Clarke spreads it: dominion is the government of heaven, earth and hell, through time and through eternity. Ellicott quotes an older divine — having added prayer to his doctrine, the apostle adds praise to his prayer — and finds the consolation: if his be the dominion, and he have called us to his glory, what can we fear?
12:
Silvanus is Silas. Gill takes him as Peter’s amanuensis or bearer or both; Robertson suspects the postscript is in Peter’s own hand, Silas having written the rest and carried it. Ellicott notes the definite article — that faithful brother unto you — and says the only doubt ever raised rests on the theory that Peter and Paul were too deeply at feud for one to patronise a friend of the other. The disputed words are as I suppose. Barnes denies any hesitation: the verb indicates firm persuasion. Ellicott makes it complete confidence, declared because there was probably disaffection towards Silas among Jewish Christians for siding with Paul. Wesley reads it as judging upon good grounds, though not by immediate inspiration; Calvin as a token of modesty. Clarke breaks with them all: Peter could never say as I suppose of Silas’s piety, so the clause belongs to the brevity — I have written to you, as I consider, briefly, by Silvanus, the faithful brother.

Where Babylon is divides the longest argument in the chapter. Gill argues for the literal city in Assyria: Peter was minister of the circumcision, Babylon was the metropolis of the Jewish dispersion, and no reason can be given why a proper name should be concealed and a figurative one used; the Rome reading is ancient, but Peter’s presence there cannot be proved. Clarke, having weighed the critics, is of the same opinion. Calvin turns it polemical: the Papists gladly lay hold on the old comment, that Peter may appear to have presided over the Church of Rome, and do not care for Christ provided Peter be left to them; and he sets against them a chronology that will not let Mark die at Alexandria in Nero’s eighth year and still leave Peter a twenty-five year Roman episcopate. Ellicott calls Rome the established interpretation, holding that nothing but prejudice can stand against the evidence that Peter died there; the name needed no explaining to Jewish readers, and prudence forbade naming a large Christian society plainly with the police so vigilant. Robertson agrees: if Peter is at Rome about the year 65, there is every reason not to make that plain to the world, least of all to Nero.

The greeter is unnamed. Barnes points out that the church that is was supplied by the translators, the Greek standing alone in the feminine, and reports two who took it of a Christian woman, perhaps Peter’s wife; Robertson thinks that the natural reading. Ellicott gives three reasons against: it is improbable that Mark was son to Peter in that sense, improbable that a wife would be put so prominently forward, and co-elect looks back to the opening of the epistle, meaning with you, not with me. Personifying a church under a female title, he adds, was becoming a not infrequent usage.

The kiss closes it. Gill notes that the Latin, Syriac and Arabic read a holy kiss, and cites Philo that a kiss and love differ, the one being possible without the other. Clarke reports the same variant in ten or twelve manuscripts and says the difference is not great. Calvin asks that the sincerity of the heart correspond with the outward act. Robertson observes that abuse of the custom confined it to men with men and women with women, and ended it at last. Cyril of Jerusalem supplies what none of the others have, the rite itself: the deacon cries aloud, receive ye one another, and let us kiss one another; think not this kiss is of the same character with those given in public by common friends, for it blends souls one with another and banishes all remembrance of wrongs; leave thy gift at the altar, be first reconciled to thy brother, then come and offer it. The kiss is reconciliation, he concludes, and for this reason holy — and he cites this very verse for it.
